title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is per-tx cap enforced even when block gas limit exceeds it?
phase1_abstract_interpretation: Abstract domain: Prysm CL validates execution payload as block-level opaque object. CL abstract state includes: beacon_state (randao, timestamp, slot), execution_payload (block_hash, parent_hash, prev_randao, timestamp, gas_limit, gas_used, transactions as opaque [][]byte). EIP-7623 property: per-tx gas cap of 16,777,216 enforced independently of block-level gas_limit. CL invariants identified: (1) ValidatePayload only checks prev_randao and timestamp - no transaction field inspection. (2) payload.Transactions treated as opaque [][]byte; CL has zero transaction deserialization code. (3) No EIP-7623 constants (16,777,216) exist in Prysm's beacon-chain/ codebase - confirmed by exhaustive search. The CL does not participate in per-tx gas cap enforcement.
phase2_symbolic_execution: Symbolic execution trace for CHK-0014: Let T_i be the i-th transaction with gas_limit(T_i). CL path: notifyNewPayload → body.Execution() → ValidatePayload → checks [prev_randao, timestamp] → RETURNS without reading T_i. EL delegation path: NewPayload(ctx, payload, ...) → rpcClient.CallContext(engine_newPayloadV4) → EL receives full payload including T_i → EL applies EIP-7623 per-tx cap check independently of block gas_limit. CL symbolic path never touches gas_limit(T_i). The enforcement occurs entirely in EL. Whether per-tx cap and block gas_limit are independently enforced is an EL specification concern, not a Prysm concern.
phase2_5_cross_component: CL/EL trust boundary analysis: Prysm sends full execution payload to EL via engine_newPayloadV4. EL is sole authority for per-tx gas cap enforcement (EIP-7623). CL trusts EL VALID/INVALID response as complete execution verdict. No secondary CL-side enforcement of per-tx caps exists - per Ethereum beacon chain specification, this is by design. The beacon chain spec does not require CL to implement EIP-7623. The EL's INVALID response is the veto mechanism for over-cap transactions, and Prysm correctly handles this response (case ErrInvalidPayloadStatus → invalidBlock{}).
phase3_invariant_proving: Property P: 'Per-tx cap is enforced independently of block.gasLimit.' Proof by architecture: (1) Prysm CL contains zero code deserializing individual transactions - confirmed by exhaustive grep of beacon-chain/core/blocks/ showing no transaction iteration. (2) Beacon chain spec does not require CL to enforce EIP-7623. (3) EL enforces via engine_newPayloadVX and returns INVALID if any tx exceeds cap. (4) Block-level gas_limit is distinct from per-tx gas cap; the EL enforces both separately. Property holds system-wide (CL+EL). CL does not independently enforce it and is architecturally correct not to do so. No gap from consensus layer perspective - EL veto is the enforcement mechanism.
phase3_5_verdict: Out of scope for Prysm consensus layer. EIP-7623 per-tx gas cap enforcement is entirely an execution-layer concern. Prysm's ValidatePayload only checks prev_randao and timestamp. The Transactions list is opaque RLP bytes from CL perspective. Engine API delegation means EL is the authoritative enforcer. Prysm's architecture is correct and consistent with Ethereum specification.
reasoning: Prysm is a consensus-layer client. The per-tx gas cap mandated by EIP-7623 is enforced by the execution layer (geth, erigon, etc.) during state transition. Prysm's CL code never deserializes individual transactions; payload.Transactions is an opaque [][]byte. ValidatePayload in beacon-chain/core/blocks/payload.go only validates prev_randao and timestamp. Per-tx gas cap enforcement is wholly outside Prysm's scope and responsibility. The EL enforces the cap and signals INVALID if violated; Prysm propagates this INVALID status correctly via invalidBlock{}.
attack_scenario: No viable attack scenario against Prysm for this property. An attacker cannot bypass EIP-7623 enforcement by manipulating Prysm's consensus logic because Prysm does not implement per-tx gas cap validation. The EL is the sole enforcement point. An attacker would need to compromise the EL to bypass this cap, which is outside Prysm's scope.
remediation: No remediation required for Prysm. Per-tx gas cap enforcement belongs in the execution layer. Prysm correctly delegates execution validity to the EL via engine_newPayloadVX and treats INVALID responses as consensus failures.

title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is gas cap validation O(1) per transaction with minimal memory?
phase1_abstract_interpretation: Abstract domain for complexity analysis: CL-side gas validation = O(0) (no gas cap code), ValidatePayload = O(1) (two field comparisons), NewPayload serialization = O(|payload|) one-time RPC cost bounded by max block size. The O(1) per-tx property is vacuously satisfied at CL level because CL performs zero per-tx gas cap iterations. No resource exhaustion attack vector exists through gas cap validation code in Prysm because no such code path exists. Payload.Transactions is never iterated for gas checking purposes.
phase2_symbolic_execution: Symbolic path for resource exhaustion: Attacker submits beacon block with payload containing N transactions with adversarial gasLimit values. CL path: ValidatePayload O(1), NewPayload O(N * avg_tx_size) for serialization. The N bound is constrained by: (a) block gas limit / minimum tx cost ≈ 30M/21000 ≈ 1428 txs max for simple transfers, (b) MaxTransactionsPerPayload = 1,048,576 (config bound), (c) MaxBytesPerTransaction = 1,073,741,824 (config bound). No unbounded loop exists in CL gas cap validation code. The EL handles the O(N) per-tx cap check internally after receiving the payload. No DoS vector specific to gas cap validation exists in Prysm's CL code.
phase2_5_cross_component: CL sends full payload to EL over Engine API (localhost IPC/HTTP). CL does not pre-filter transactions before forwarding. EL's per-tx gas cap check is an EL concern. CL contribution to validation complexity is O(1) for CL-validated fields. Engine API RPC is O(|payload|) for serialization, bounded by block byte size. No Prysm-specific O(N^2) or unbounded complexity path exists for gas cap validation. The CL-side resource use is bounded and not exploitable via per-tx gas cap manipulation.
phase3_invariant_proving: Property P: 'Gas cap validation is O(1) per transaction with minimal memory.' For Prysm CL: Gas cap validation complexity = O(0) - no such code exists. Payload forwarding = O(|payload|) one-time cost. ValidatePayload = O(1). The O(1) per-tx property cannot be violated in code that never executes per-tx loops. No memory allocation per transaction for gas cap purposes occurs in CL. Property holds trivially by absence of the validation code in question.
phase3_5_verdict: Out of scope for Prysm. No per-tx gas cap validation code exists in Prysm's consensus layer. The O(1) complexity requirement applies to EL implementations. Prysm's payload handling is O(1) for CL-validated fields and O(|payload|) for serialization, which is irreducible and bounded by protocol constants (MaxBytesPerTransaction, MaxTransactionsPerPayload).
reasoning: Prysm does not implement per-tx gas cap validation, making the O(1) complexity requirement vacuously satisfied at the CL level. This property is an EL concern. Prysm's CL-side payload processing is O(1) for consensus field validation and O(|payload|) for EL delegation. No DoS vector from gas cap validation logic exists in Prysm because there is no gas cap validation logic to exploit.
attack_scenario: No viable attack scenario. An attacker cannot exploit O(N^2) gas cap validation behavior in code that does not exist. Block size is bounded by MaxTransactionsPerPayload (1,048,576) and MaxBytesPerTransaction (1,073,741,824), providing natural DoS protection for the serialization cost.
remediation: No remediation required. This is an EL concern. Prysm's bounded payload handling is correct.

title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does block validation catch over-cap transactions from direct block construction?
phase1_abstract_interpretation: Abstract domain for Engine API trust boundary: Execution payload arrives at Prysm via P2P gossip (beacon block) or local MEV builder path (getPayload). Payload.Transactions is opaque [][]byte containing RLP-encoded txs. MEV builders construct blocks bypassing standard txpool. CL role: (1) validate consensus-layer fields, (2) send to EL via engine_newPayloadVX, (3) accept/reject based on EL response. Invariant: EL INVALID response is definitive veto for any execution violation including over-cap transactions. Abstract state: EL_validity(payload) ∈ {VALID, INVALID, SYNCING}. Prysm maps: VALID→(true,nil), SYNCING→(false,nil) [optimistic], INVALID→(false,invalidBlock{}).
phase2_symbolic_execution: Attack path - MEV builder with over-cap transactions: (1) MEV builder constructs block with tx T where gasLimit(T) > EIP-7623_CAP=16,777,216. (2) Block propagates to Prysm via P2P as beacon block containing this payload. (3) Prysm calls notifyNewPayload → reaches NewPayload(ctx, payload, ...). (4) EL receives engine_newPayloadV4 call with full payload. (5) EL applies EIP-7623: gasLimit(T) > CAP → state transition fails → EL returns PayloadStatus_INVALID. (6) NewPayload maps PayloadStatus_INVALID → returns ErrInvalidPayloadStatus. (7) notifyNewPayload switch case: errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidPayloadStatus) → returns (false, invalidBlock{error: ErrInvalidPayload, lastValidHash: lvh}). (8) Prysm marks block invalid and prunes it via pruneInvalidBlock. Edge case: Optimistic sync (ErrAcceptedSyncingPayloadStatus) → returns (false, nil) → block optimistically accepted temporarily. This applies equally to ALL EL violations, not EIP-7623-specific. When EL catches up, it will retroactively invalidate.
phase2_5_cross_component: Trust boundary analysis - Engine API MEV builder bypass: External actors (MEV builders) do NOT directly call Prysm's Engine API. The Engine API endpoint is authenticated via JWT token on localhost between CL and local EL. MEV builders submit blocks via MEV-boost relay network → CL receives payload → CL forwards to local EL via authenticated engine_newPayloadV4. Therefore: (a) External actors cannot inject payloads bypassing EL validation. (b) CL-EL Engine API trust boundary is intact via JWT authentication. (c) EL INVALID response for over-cap transactions correctly handled by notifyNewPayload. (d) No bypass path exists at CL level. System correctly relies on EL enforcement with CL relay of INVALID responses. The check_id notes 'MEV block builders could bypass txpool' - this is accurate for txpool, but does NOT bypass EL state transition validation, which is the enforcement point for over-cap txs.
phase3_invariant_proving: Property P: 'Block validation catches over-cap transactions from Engine API block construction.' Proof by code trace: (1) All blocks with over-cap transactions → EL returns PayloadStatus_INVALID. (2) NewPayload maps INVALID → ErrInvalidPayloadStatus (engine_client.go line ~196 result.Status check). (3) notifyNewPayload handles ErrInvalidPayloadStatus → returns invalidBlock{error: ErrInvalidPayload, lastValidHash: lvh}. (4) invalidBlock error propagates up through onBlockBatch → handleInvalidExecutionError → pruneInvalidBlock. (5) Block is rejected and pruned. Property holds through EL delegation. Exception: ErrAcceptedSyncingPayloadStatus (SYNCING) → block optimistically accepted. However: (a) this is standard optimistic sync behavior for ALL blocks during EL sync, (b) not specific to EIP-7623, (c) retroactively corrected when EL finishes syncing. This exception does not constitute a vulnerability against Prysm.
phase3_5_verdict: Not a vulnerability in Prysm. The property 'block validation catches over-cap transactions from Engine API' holds through correct EL delegation. Prysm's notifyNewPayload properly relays the EL's INVALID response for over-cap transactions and marks the block as invalid. The optimistic sync exception applies uniformly to all execution violations and is not EIP-7623-specific. Architecture is correct per Ethereum specifications.
reasoning: Prysm's notifyNewPayload correctly handles EL INVALID responses for all execution violations including EIP-7623 per-tx cap violations. Lines 281-289 of execution_engine.go map EL PayloadStatus_INVALID → ErrInvalidPayloadStatus → invalidBlock{} → block pruning. MEV builders cannot bypass EL validation because payloads always flow through the local EL via the authenticated Engine API (JWT-secured localhost endpoint). The optimistic sync path (SYNCING response) is standard behavior applicable to all EL rules, not a gap specific to EIP-7623.
attack_scenario: Theoretical attack: MEV builder constructs block with tx gasLimit > EIP-7623 cap, propagates via P2P. Actual result: EL returns INVALID → notifyNewPayload returns invalidBlock → Prysm rejects and prunes the block. Attack fails. Only partial-bypass: optimistic sync mode (EL is syncing). This is temporary and retroactively corrects when EL catches up - not EIP-7623-specific. No actionable vulnerability in Prysm.
remediation: No remediation required. Existing INVALID handling in notifyNewPayload is sufficient. Architecture correctly delegates per-tx cap enforcement to the EL and correctly handles the INVALID response.

title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does transaction replacement re-validate gasLimit?
phase1_abstract_interpretation: Abstract domain for txpool TOCTOU: A TOCTOU vulnerability in transaction replacement requires: (1) Tx T_old admitted to txpool with valid gasLimit. (2) Tx T_new replaces T_old (same nonce, higher gasPrice) with invalid gasLimit > EIP-7623_CAP. (3) Re-validation skipped → T_new enters txpool with invalid gasLimit → included in block without EL catching it at inclusion time. Searching Prysm: zero txpool/mempool code in beacon-chain/. The testing/endtoend/ code invokes geth RPC APIs for e2e testing but does not implement txpool logic. Prysm has no transaction admission, replacement, or re-validation mechanism.
phase2_symbolic_execution: Symbolic path for txpool TOCTOU: This path does not exist in Prysm's codebase. Transaction replacement (eth_sendRawTransaction to txpool, nonce replacement logic) is handled entirely by the execution layer. The consensus layer receives finalized transaction lists in execution payloads after the EL block builder selects transactions. Prysm never participates in txpool management. No symbolic path through Prysm code reaches any transaction replacement or re-validation logic. The attack would need to operate at the EL level.
phase2_5_cross_component: CL/EL boundary for transactions: EL maintains txpool → EL builds block (getPayload) → CL receives payload with finalized tx list → CL validates consensus fields → CL delegates execution validity to EL (newPayload). There is no txpool exposure at CL boundary. Even if EL txpool had a TOCTOU bug allowing over-cap tx through replacement, the EL's state transition function (called during newPayload) would catch the over-cap tx and return INVALID. This is a layered defense: (1) txpool validation (first check), (2) state transition validation during newPayload (authoritative check). Prysm is not involved in either check.
phase3_invariant_proving: Property P: 'Transaction replacement re-validates gasLimit to prevent TOCTOU.' For Prysm: Vacuously satisfied - no txpool code exists. For EL (out of scope): Must hold in geth/erigon txpool - when replacement tx is submitted, EL must re-validate gasLimit. Even if this fails in txpool, the EL state transition (newPayload) provides a second check. No attack surface for this property exists in Prysm's codebase.
phase3_5_verdict: Out of scope for Prysm. Transaction replacement and txpool validation are exclusively execution-layer concerns. No txpool code exists in Prysm's beacon-chain implementation. This should be evaluated against the EL client (geth, erigon, etc.).
reasoning: Prysm is a consensus-layer client with no txpool implementation. Transaction replacement TOCTOU vulnerabilities are only possible in txpool code, which lives entirely in the execution layer. Prysm receives completed execution payloads with finalized transaction lists; it never participates in transaction admission, replacement, or re-validation. This checklist item should be evaluated against the EL client.
attack_scenario: No attack scenario applicable to Prysm. Any txpool TOCTOU vulnerability would need to be evaluated against the execution layer client (geth/erigon). Even if the txpool were bypassed, the EL state transition function during engine_newPayloadVX would catch over-cap transactions and return INVALID.
remediation: No remediation required for Prysm. If this is a concern, evaluate the EL client's txpool replacement logic and EIP-7623 gasLimit validation in geth/erigon.

title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is gasLimit covered by the transaction signature?
phase1_abstract_interpretation: Abstract domain for signature coverage analysis: EL transaction signing hash coverage is defined by EIP specifications. For all current Ethereum transaction types: Legacy (EIP-155): rlp([nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data, v, r, s]) - gasLimit INCLUDED. EIP-2930 (type 1): rlp([chainId, nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data, accessList]) - gasLimit INCLUDED. EIP-1559 (type 2): rlp([chainId, nonce, maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas, gasLimit, to, value, data, accessList]) - gasLimit INCLUDED. EIP-4844 (type 3): extends EIP-1559 with blob fields - gasLimit INCLUDED. Prysm's CL: payload.Transactions is opaque [][]byte. Prysm has zero transaction deserialization code, zero ECDSA/secp256k1 signature verification code for EL transactions. The signature coverage property is an EL and EIP specification concern.
phase2_symbolic_execution: Attack path for signature exclusion: (1) Attacker creates tx T where gasLimit is excluded from signing hash. (2) Attacker signs T, then modifies gasLimit after signing. (3) T submitted to EL txpool. (4) EL admits T if signature verification does not cover gasLimit. (5) T included in block by EL. (6) Prysm receives beacon block with T in payload.Transactions. (7) Prysm CL path: payload.Transactions treated as [][]byte opaque → ValidatePayload checks prev_randao, timestamp → NewPayload sends payload to EL → EL processes state transition including T (T was already admitted without signature re-verification at execution time). Prysm is not in any part of this attack path. The vulnerability (if real) would manifest in EL's txpool signature verification and signing hash computation, entirely outside Prysm's scope.
phase2_5_cross_component: Cross-component analysis: Ethereum transaction signing (EIP-155, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-4844) requires gasLimit to be in the signing hash by specification. This is enforced by the EL during txpool admission. CL's role: include transaction list (received from local EL via getPayload or MEV-boost) in beacon block - CL never modifies transaction content. The property 'gasLimit is covered by signature' is an EL transaction format invariant. Prysm cannot enforce this because it never deserializes EL transaction data. CL cannot detect post-signing modification of gasLimit because it treats the entire transaction as an opaque byte array.
phase3_invariant_proving: Property P: 'gasLimit is covered by transaction signature, preventing post-signing modification.' For Prysm: Property is entirely outside Prysm's scope. No transaction deserialization, no ECDSA signature verification code for EL transactions, no mechanism to check gasLimit field coverage. Confirmed by: (1) beacon-chain/core/blocks/signature.go handles only BLS signatures on beacon objects. (2) No secp256k1 or ECDSA code in beacon-chain/. (3) payload.Transactions deserialization code absent. For all current Ethereum transaction types (Legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-4844): gasLimit IS included in signing hash per specification. The property must be enforced by: (a) EIP specification mandating gasLimit in signing hash, (b) EL correctly computing signing hash, (c) EL txpool rejecting invalid signatures.
phase3_5_verdict: Out of scope for Prysm. Transaction signature coverage of gasLimit is an Ethereum transaction format and EL state transition concern. Prysm has no transaction signature verification code for EL transactions. The opaque handling of payload.Transactions is architecturally correct per beacon chain specification.
reasoning: Prysm is a consensus-layer client that treats execution layer transactions as opaque bytes. It never inspects, deserializes, or verifies ECDSA signatures on EL transactions. The property 'gasLimit is covered by transaction signature' is enforced by the EL during transaction admission (txpool) and state transition (engine_newPayloadVX). Prysm's signature.go only handles BLS signatures on beacon chain objects (blocks, attestations, voluntary exits, sync committees). All current Ethereum transaction types (EIP-155, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-4844) include gasLimit in their signing hashes by specification.
attack_scenario: No attack scenario applicable to Prysm. If gasLimit were excluded from the EL transaction signing hash (an EIP specification or EL implementation bug), an attacker could modify gasLimit after signing at the EL level. This is entirely unrelated to Prysm's CL logic. The vulnerability, if it existed, would affect the EL state transition function, not Prysm.
remediation: No remediation required for Prysm. Transaction signature coverage is an EL and EIP specification concern. All current Ethereum transaction types include gasLimit in their signing hashes. If concerned, audit the EL client's transaction signing and verification code.
